n: Ezekiel is carried in a vision by the Spirit to a valley strewn with bones—perhaps the scene of an ancient battle where the dead were never buried. “The hand of the LORD” signals a powerful revelatory experience.

f.w: The hand of the LORD was upon me
in the spirit of the LORD

n: God walks Ezekiel all around the valley so he can see how many bones there are and how completely dead they are. Humanly speaking, the situation is hopeless.

f.g: Long dead—no trace of life remains.

n: “Can these bones live?” Ezekiel’s wise answer neither doubts nor presumes: only God knows what God can do.
The prophet is told to preach to dead bones—an absurd task unless God’s word itself carries life-giving power.

f.w: hear the word of the LORD

n: The Hebrew word ruach means breath, wind, and spirit, and this chapter plays on all three meanings. God promises to put breath back into the dead.

f.g: Hebrew ruach—breath, wind, or spirit; the same word appears throughout this vision.

n: The order follows the human body—sinews, flesh, skin, then breath. Like the creation of Adam, the body is formed first and then given life.

f.g: Tendons and ligaments that hold bones together.

n: As Ezekiel obeys, there is a rattling, and bones snap into place, each to its proper partner. God’s word is already working.

f.g: Or “a rattling”; Hebrew raʿash, also used for an earthquake.

n: The bodies are complete but still lifeless. The vision shows two stages: physical restoration, then the gift of life.
Ezekiel is told to summon the breath from the four winds—from every direction. God’s Spirit is the true source of life.

f.w: Come from the four winds, O breath

n: Breath enters, and the dead stand up as a vast army. Latter-day Saints also see in this vision a vivid picture of the literal resurrection, when spirit and body are reunited.

f.w: they lived, and stood up upon their feet

n: God interprets the vision. The bones are exiled Israel, who feel dead, hopeless, and cut off. Ezekiel’s audience in Babylon was quoting its own despair back to God.

f.g: “We are completely cut off”—a cry of despair.

n: Their “graves” are the lands of exile. God promises to open them and bring His people home—a national resurrection that also points to the literal resurrection of the dead.
When Israel is raised and returned, they will finally recognize the Lord’s power and love. The tender phrase “O my people” is repeated.
The climax: God will put His own Spirit in them. Physical return is not enough; true life comes when God’s Spirit dwells in His people.

f.w: shall put my spirit in you

f.g: God both promises and carries out what He says.

n: A second revelation follows, this time an object lesson Ezekiel is to act out.

Ezekiel writes on two sticks (or wooden tablets): one for Judah, one for Joseph through Ephraim. In history, these represent the southern and northern kingdoms. Latter-day Saints also understand them as records—the Bible (record of Judah) and the Book of Mormon (record of Joseph).

f.g: Hebrew ʿets—wood; possibly a wooden writing board, as used in the ancient Near East.

f.w: For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim

n: Joined end to end in Ezekiel’s hand, the two sticks look like one. Israel, long divided, will be united—and Latter-day Saints see the two records growing together as one witness of Christ.

f.w: they shall become one in thine hand

n: The exiles will ask what this strange act means. Ezekiel’s symbolic actions were designed to provoke questions.

f.w: Wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest

n: God Himself will join Joseph’s stick with Judah’s. The unity is His work, not merely a human arrangement.

f.w: they shall be one in mine hand

n: Ezekiel holds the sticks up before the people—a visible, memorable sign of the promise.
Gathering again: God will bring the scattered children of Israel from every nation back to their land.
Israel had been split into two kingdoms since about 930 BC. God promises that the division will end under one king.

f.w: they shall be no more two nations

n: Unity will come with purity. A gathered people will also be a cleansed people, free from idols.
“David my servant” cannot be David himself, who had died centuries earlier. It refers to a future king from David’s line—fulfilled supremely in Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd.

f.w: David my servant shall be king over them

n: The promised land is a lasting inheritance for generation after generation, under the rule of the Davidic prince forever.

A “covenant of peace” and “everlasting covenant” brings God’s sanctuary—His temple presence—into their midst. Latter-day Saints connect the everlasting covenant with the restored gospel and temple blessings.
God will dwell among His people. John’s Revelation echoes this promise as the ultimate destiny of the faithful.

f.w: My tabernacle also shall be with them

n: The presence of God’s temple among Israel will show the world that He has made them holy. The chapter ends with the theme that runs through Ezekiel’s final chapters: God’s presence returning to His people.

f.g: Make holy; set apart for God.
